title: O House of Atika, Which I Shun
intro: Al-Ahwas wrote this in praise of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, the future caliph, while Umar was governor of Medina. Abu al-Faraj relates in al-Aghani that Umar's brother Abu Bakr had promised to take the poet with him to the caliph in Syria and then went back on his word; Umar sent for al-Ahwas, gave him money and clothes, and asked him to leave his brother's honour alone. Al-Ahwas answered with this poem, set to the meter of one by Sulayman ibn Abi Dubakil that begins “O house of Khansa', which I shun”, and when he recited it Umar said, “You have not spared me what I asked to be spared”, for the poem praised Umar and, by implication, faulted his brother. It opens with the house of Atika, which the poet avoids for fear of slanderers while his heart stays there, mourns his lost youth, answers a woman who scolds him for staying at home by saying that Umar has spared him the journey, and praises a governor who keeps his word where others broke theirs. “The house of Atika” became a proverb for a place one turns away from while the heart turns towards it, and al-Baghdadi tells how a young man of Medina quoted the opening to the caliph al-Mansur to remind him of an unpaid gift, so that al-Mansur recalled the line “I see you do what you say” and paid twice over.

translation: O house of Atika, which I shun
for fear of enemies, though my heart is pledged to it,
1.sharh: He keeps away from the house of the woman he loves so that his enemies have nothing to say, but his heart never leaves it. The commentator al-Marzuqi set it beside a line of the same thought in Abu Tammam's anthology: “I turn my camels from the road to her people, while my heart heads straight for her.”

translation: I have come to give you coldness, and yet,
I swear, for all the coldness, I lean towards you more.
2.sharh: He shows the house nothing but coldness, and swears that he loves it all the more. Apart from its rhyme word, the line is word for word a line of Sulayman ibn Abi Dubakil's, whose poem al-Ahwas took as his model.

translation: You have taken a place in my heart
where no one but you has ever stayed.
3.sharh: No one has ever held the place in his heart that the house holds; he avoids it outwardly, but it alone lives there. As in the lines around it, he speaks to the house and means the woman inside; one anthology addresses her directly, in the feminine.

translation: I have told you of some of my longing,
and what I have kept hidden is longer still.
4.sharh: What he has confessed of his love is only part of it; far more stays unspoken. A lover who is watched learns to keep most of his feeling to himself.

translation: I turned from you, but not out of hatred:
I fear the talk of a spiteful man who has no sense.
5.sharh: He stays away for fear of a spiteful gossip, not because his love has cooled. Other sources read “who never sleeps”: a watcher who misses nothing.

translation: Will our life with you, in your days, come back?
since you, my search for comfort has faltered.
6.sharh: He asks whether the days spent near the house will return; since then nothing has consoled him. Other sources read “since you, every comfort has turned ugly”.

translation: Whenever I say, “He has come right,” perversity
drags him down, as a squint-eyed man looks askew.
7.sharh: He means the spiteful man of line 5: whenever he seems to have mended his ways, he turns crooked again, as a cross-eyed man cannot look straight however hard he tries.

translation: Had what I spent to soften his heart, which would not soften,
been spent on stone, the stone would have softened.
8.sharh: The effort he spent trying to win over the spiteful man would have softened rock. The commentator al-Baghdadi takes “his heart” as the enemy's, which makes him harder than stone.

translation: Shunning the house of the one I love,
to please the one I hate, is a hard thing to bear.
9.sharh: He avoids the house he loves only to please the enemy he hates, and finds it a bitter, baffling thing to do to himself. The lover punishes himself so that the slanderer has nothing to say.

translation: And though I turn away, you are, but for my fear,
dearer to me than the houses I visit and enter.
10.sharh: He tells the house that it is dearer to him than every house he calls at; only caution keeps him away. His other visits are a cover.

translation: Youth, and the sweet life
that made us happy and glad for a time:
11.sharh: Youth and the pleasures of youth are the subject of a sentence that runs on through the next two lines: both are gone. He sets them side by side so as to mourn them together.

translation: its cheer has gone, and the memory of it has become
a grief the heart drinks again and again,
12.sharh: Youth has lost its bloom, and remembering it is now a grief he drinks over and over. What once gave joy now gives pain. Some sources read “its cheer has fled” and “a sorrow”.

translation: but for remembering what is past, and a longing
fated to an enthralled heart that cannot forget.
13.sharh: Nothing is left of youth but memories and a longing he cannot shake off. Everything else has gone; only the remembering and the yearning stay, fixed in a heart enslaved by love.

translation: Youth is gone, its pleasures worn thin,
and I am the one who grieves and wails for youth,
14.sharh: His youth has died and its pleasures have worn out like old clothes, and he mourns it aloud as one mourns the dead. He elegises his own youth as he would a friend.

translation: weeping for the new that time has turned
to old; and time is nothing to lean on.
15.sharh: He weeps because time has worn out what was new, then checks himself: time is not to be trusted. “Wails” and “lean on” in the two rhymes come from the same Arabic root, a play the translation cannot keep.

translation: And whiteness covers my head, as though, after the black,
a year-old thagham plant grew on it.
16.sharh: His hair has turned completely white, like the thagham once it has bleached. Grey hair and the thagham are an old pairing in Arabic verse, and the whitening is the work of the time he has just lamented.

translation: Many a foolish woman has risen against me before dawn,
blaming me in her ignorance for staying, and scolding,
17.sharh: A woman wakes him before dawn to scold him for staying at home instead of travelling to seek his fortune. The scolding woman is a stock figure of Arabic poetry; here she gives the poet his way into the praise of Umar.

translation: and I answered her by saying, “You will not be obeyed,
so leave off your counsel, which will not be taken.”
18.sharh: He tells her that her advice will not be followed and she may as well stop. In his eyes her concern is ignorance: she does not know that Umar has already provided for him, as the next line says.

translation: Umar has spared me the toil of a journey
and the rebuff of the mean and miserly
19.sharh: He has no need to travel in search of a patron: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, close at hand in Medina, has spared him the road and the cold shoulder of misers.

translation: with the gifts of a generous man whose buckets
overflow for all when a barren season comes.
20.sharh: Umar's generosity reaches everyone, like water drawn in plenty in a year of drought. He gives most when others give least, when the land is barren and people need it most.

translation: Undaunted by strange events, as though he were
a gleaming, keen sword the burnisher has polished.
21.sharh: He meets sudden and unheard-of troubles without hesitating, sharp and bright as a freshly polished sword. Comparing a patron to a sword is among the oldest images of Arabic praise.

translation: When he appears, men show their awe of him
as small birds fear the falcon swooping on them.
22.sharh: Men stand in awe of him the moment he appears, as small birds cower when a falcon dives at them. Another source has “men lower their eyes”, out of respect.

translation: They see that he stands above them in rank and power,
with a merit, his from the first, that none can deny.
23.sharh: Everyone acknowledges that he outranks them, and that his merit was his before anyone else's. His standing is settled; no one disputes it.

translation: He shoulders the weight of affairs; a forebear
ahead in goodness won him the lead in noble deeds.
24.sharh: He carries heavy burdens, and his precedence in nobility is inherited: ancestors who went first in doing good secured it for him. His honour is old, not newly made.

translation: And when Quraysh are traced to their roots, among them
his is the glory of descent and the finest deeds.
25.sharh: Among the clans of Quraysh, the Prophet's tribe and the Umayyads' own, he has both the noblest lineage and the noblest conduct, and does not rely on one without the other.

translation: I had first sought the friendship of men
who made promises, and broke them when put to the test,
26.sharh: He had first looked to other patrons, who promised much and failed him once their word was tested. He means Umar's brother Abu Bakr: Ibn Asakir, quoting the lines that follow, says al-Ahwas was hinting at him.

translation: until certainty turned my hopes
to despair, and those I hoped in failed me.
27.sharh: In time he was sure there was nothing to hope for from them: experience, not suspicion, taught him. The sentence ends in the next line.

translation: I left what they had done and came to you in haste;
with you there is refuge from them.
28.sharh: Done with them, he hurried to Umar, in whom he finds a refuge from those who let him down. “In haste” shows how eagerly he turned to Umar once he had given up on the others.

translation: You made me a promise in my need and kept it,
true when they lied in their words and went back on them.
29.sharh: Umar promised and delivered, while the others lied and changed their minds. The line sets his good faith against their bad faith, and the others again include his brother Abu Bakr.

translation: I will thank you for what you have done for me
with thanks the camels carry wherever they halt or set out:
30.sharh: He swears to thank Umar so widely that his gratitude will be heard wherever people travel. Poems spread with travellers and caravans, so the image is close to literal.

translation: praise poems whose rarest lines are given to you
freely, and to no one else.
31.sharh: His finest verse will go to Umar and his house alone. Al-Buhturi's anthology quotes the line in the third person, “to him”.

translation: When I sift my verse,
the best of what I choose is yours.
32.sharh: Whenever he picks out the best of his poetry, the best goes to Umar and his house. With the line before, it makes one promise: no one else will be praised with his finest verse.

translation: I will praise you as long as I live, and if I die
its rare lines will live on for you, quoted as proverbs.
33.sharh: He will praise them all his life, and the praise will outlive him in lines people go on repeating. He was right: decades later, a young man of Medina used the poem to jog the caliph al-Mansur's memory.

translation: By the life of Him to whose House the pilgrims go,
borne swiftly by young camels at an easy pace,
34.sharh: He swears by God, Lord of the Kaaba to which pilgrims hurry on young camels. The oath is completed in the next line, which reminds Umar of the kinship between them.

translation: a man who has won kinship with you
and seeks his gain from others is misled.
35.sharh: Anyone related to Umar who looks for favours elsewhere has lost his way. The poet counts himself among Umar's kin, so Umar is the only patron he needs.

translation: You forgive them with your forbearance when they behave like fools,
and when they ask for gifts you give, and give lavishly.
36.sharh: Umar is patient with his people when they wrong him, and generous when they ask. Whoever offends him meets forbearance, and whoever asks of him meets generosity.

translation: You are their stronghold when nothing
but a stronghold can save them from what they dread,
37.sharh: When danger comes and only a fortress can save them, he is that fortress. The word “stronghold” opens the line and closes it, to say that he is their only refuge.

translation: until you seem, as they shelter behind you,
a grim lion of Bisha crouched in its den.
38.sharh: His people hide behind him as behind a lion, fierce and ready, guarding its lair. He protects them as surely as he frightens their enemies.

translation: I see you do what you say, while some of them
are false of tongue, saying what they do not do.
39.sharh: Umar keeps his word, unlike others whose word cannot be trusted. This is the hint at his brother that the Aghani's account turns on; the critics Ibn Rashiq cites faulted the line, since a ruler should not be praised for doing what he must.

1.1.3.meaning: Atika: an Umayyad lady whom poets courted in verse. Al-Baghdadi makes her the daughter of the caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya and wife of Abd al-Malik; the editor Jamal, a granddaughter of Yazid.

1.2.5.head: مُوَكَّل
1.2.5.meaning: Pledged: put in its charge, so that the heart never leaves it.

3.2.4-5.meaning: “In it, ever”: the editions have instead “by my faith” (wa-l-amana), an oath: by my faith, no one else has stayed there.

5.2.3.head: كاشِح
5.2.3.meaning: Kashih: an enemy who hides his hatred, literally “one who turns his flank”.

6.2.4.head: المُتَعَلِّل
6.2.4.meaning: One who distracts or comforts himself with something.

7.2.5.head: الأَقبَل
7.2.5.meaning: Aqbal: a man whose eyes turn in towards his nose, a kind of squint.

10.1.5.head: رِقبَة
10.1.5.meaning: Riqba: wariness, fear of being watched.

12.2.2-5.meaning: “The heart is given its second drink and its first”: herders watered camels twice, the nahal and the alal; the heart drinks grief again and again.

16.2.4.head: الثَّغام
16.2.4.meaning: Thagham: a plant, green at first, that turns white when it dries.

17.1.1.head: سَفيهَة
17.1.1.meaning: “And many a foolish woman”: the “and” here means “many a”.

19.2.1.head: عُمَر
19.2.1.meaning: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, then the Umayyad governor of Medina, later caliph (99–101 AH, 717–720 CE).

20.1.5.head: سِجال
20.1.5.meaning: Sijal: great buckets full of water; here, his gifts.

22.2.2.head: البُغاث
22.2.2.meaning: Bughath: small birds that do not hunt.

23.1.5.head: سَورَة
23.1.5.meaning: Sawra: height of rank, and power over others.

24.2.4.head: مُتَمَهِّل
24.2.4.meaning: Ahead in goodness: the dictionaries give tamahhul as going first.

26.2.5.head: حُصِّلَ
26.2.5.meaning: Put to the test: literally “sifted”, their worth brought out.

30.2.2-5.meaning: “The mounts halt and set off with it”: travellers carry it wherever they go.

32.1.2.head: تَنَخَّلَ
32.1.2.meaning: Sifted: chose the best of it, as flour is sifted.

33.2.4.head: تَمَثَّلَ
33.2.4.meaning: Quoted as proverbs, cited to fit the moment.

34.1.1.head: لَعَمر
34.1.1.meaning: “By the life of”: a form of oath.

38.2.3.head: بيشَة
38.2.3.meaning: Bisha: a place known for its lions.

38.2.4.head: خادِر
38.2.4.meaning: Khadir: a lion that keeps to its lair.

39.2.1-2.meaning: “Watered-down of tongue”: one who mixes lies with truth, as milk is mixed with water. Most sources have “watered-down of speech”.
